## Introduction

Lung function is a useful indicator of respiratory health surveillance in children and is predictive of long-term outcomes including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and early mortality in adulthood.1 2 Lung development begins around 4 weeks gestation and, while it continues through early adulthood, most structural development occurs in the fetal and early postnatal life-stages.3 Lung function trajectories tend to remain stable over time; low lung function in early life is predictive of low lung function in early adulthood, a known risk factor for poor health outcomes.4 Reduced lung function in childhood has also been identified as a risk factor for persistent asthma, an asthma phenotype where symptoms begin in early childhood and continue into adolescence or adulthood.5

Given the known course of lung development, characterizing prenatal risk factors for low lung function and persistent lung disease is of great public health interest. A growing literature suggests that gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), defined as glucose intolerance that develops during pregnancy among women who have not been previously diagnosed with diabetes, may be a prenatal risk factor for respiratory disease in children.6 7 8 GDM is a common pregnancy complication affecting 6–9% of pregnancies in the U.S and is associated with numerous adverse outcomes during pregnancy, delivery, and in offspring.9 10 While the mechanism linking GDM to early lung development and subsequent respiratory outcomes is unknown, intrauterine processes related to GDM such as hyperglycemia, placental inflammation, altered immune response and oxidative stress during susceptible windows of fetal lung development may be contributing factors.11 12

Building on existing evidence, the present study examines the association between GDM and lung function at 8–9 years of age in a well-characterized, socioeconomically and racially diverse, prospective U.S. pregnancy cohort. With the exception of one recent study,13 prior studies on GDM and respiratory health have focused on clinical outcomes such as asthma or wheeze;6–8 14–17 these studies also tend to focus on young pediatric populations that may be experiencing transient asthma-like disease that is different from conditions experienced by older children. Lung function tests are objective measurements that provide a novel means of assessing the relationship between GDM and child respiratory health, beyond reported diagnoses or symptoms. Here, we investigate the association between GDM and lung function in mid-childhood, as well as current asthma and wheeze, to provide insights into how GDM may related to a broad continuum of respiratory health outcomes.

## Methods

### Study Population

We studied mother-child dyads participating in the Conditions Affecting Neurocognitive Development in Early Childhood (CANDLE) study, a prospective pregnancy cohort study based in Shelby County, Tennessee. Eligibility and enrollment criteria have been previously described.6 18 19 In brief, CANDLE staff enrolled women during the second trimester of pregnancy (16 to 28 gestational weeks). Eligible women had singleton pregnancies that were determined to be medically low-risk, i.e., pregnancies had no evidence of certain conditions at enrollment, including chronic hypertension requiring medication, oligohydramnios, or insulin-dependent (type-1) diabetes.18 All women were 16 to 40 years of age, spoke English and planned to deliver at a study hospital. Births occurred between December 2006 and June 2011. Women enrolled in CANDLE responded to questionnaires and provided biospecimens during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy and at delivery. Study staff also performed medical record abstraction to document pregnancy and delivery characteristics.18 Dyads participated in follow-up clinic visits at child age 1, 2 and 3 years, at approximately 4.5 years and approximately 8–9 years.

CANDLE includes 1503 total enrolled dyads, 911 of whom participated in the 8–9 year follow-up. A total of 799 pulmonary function tests (PFT) were administered at the 8–9 year follow-up visit, of which 740 were designated as acceptable effort by pediatric pulmonologist review. The current analysis includes dyads with documented GDM status, gestational age of delivery ≥ 32 weeks and acceptable 8–9 year pulmonary function test data (n=722) or 8–9 year respiratory outcome questionnaire assessment (n=892). We did not identify any women with existing (pre-pregnancy) type 2 diabetes in this sample; 16 multiparous women reported “yes” to ever having diabetes (unspecified type) at enrollment but did not report having diabetes currently. This response likely reflects having GDM in a prior pregnancy, not ongoing pre-pregnancy diabetes.6 Women with type 1 diabetes were not included since they were not eligible to enroll in CANDLE. Women provided written informed consent for themselves and their children through 8–9 year follow-up; at age 8–9 follow-up, children also provided assent for themselves. The study was approved by relevant academic Institutional Review Boards.

### Gestational Diabetes Assessment

Pregnancy complications and medical updates, including diagnosis of GDM, were assessed via maternal interview after delivery. All information was confirmed by CANDLE study nurses through chart abstraction of medical records that were provided by study hospitals.6 18

### Childhood Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)

Trained CANDLE staff administered PFTs using Breezesuite™ software and American Thoracic Society (ATS) guidelines, as previously described.19 Each participant attempted between 3 and 8 lung function assessments. Children with respiratory infections, difficulty breathing, use of asthma rescue medication in the previous 3 days, or more than one nighttime asthma attack in the previous 4 weeks were rescheduled. Outcomes derived from PFT tests included 1) forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1); 2) forced vital capacity (FVC); 3) the ratio of FEV1 to FVC (FEV1/FVC) and 4) forced expiratory flow between 25% and 75% of the vital capacity (FEF25–75). We calculated FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC z-scores using 2022 Global Lung Institute (GLI) race-neutral reference equations (GLI-Global, 2022), standardized by subject sex, height and age to a reference population.20 We calculated FEF25–75 z-scores using the 2012 GLI-Other reference equations because this outcome was not included in the 2022 update.21

### Childhood respiratory outcome questionnaire

Parents completed a questionnaire based on the International Study of Asthma and Allergies in Children (ISAAC) and other questions to assess current wheeze and current asthma at age 8–9 years.22 The majority of questionnaires (795 of 892, 89%) were completed in person during study visits; 97 were administered online due to restrictions on in-person study visits during the Covid-19 pandemic. Similar to our prior assessment of asthma and wheeze at age 4–6 years,6 we defined current wheeze as parent-report of a child experiencing wheezing or whistling in the chest in the previous 12 months, in the absence of a cold.22 We defined current asthma as having at least 2 of the following (1) current wheeze (as defined), (2) report of provider diagnosis of asthma or reactive airway disease (ever), or (3) report of asthma-specific medication use in the previous 12 months.

### Covariates

Women self-reported demographic and health history information at enrollment during the 2nd trimester of pregnancy, including age (years), race (American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, Black, Native Hawaiian/other Pacific Islander, White, other, or multiple), ethnicity (Hispanic, Non-Hispanic), asthma history (yes, no), prenatal smoking (yes, no), pre-pregnancy weight and height, and education (less than high school, high school, some college, 4-year college degree, or post-graduate degree). We measured urinary cotinine in maternal samples provided at second and third trimester study visits.23 Maternal prenatal smoking was defined as either self-reported smoking or specific gravity-adjusted urinary cotinine > 200 ng/ml at either time point.24 Parity was determined at enrollment and dichotomized for analysis as ≥1 prior live birth or none; maternal race was collapsed into two categories for analysis (Black and non-Black). Pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI) was calculated using self-reported weight and height as kg/m2. We determined child sex and gestational age from labor and delivery forms. We estimated gestational weight gain as the difference between self-reported pre-pregnancy weight and weight at delivery in the medical record. Trained staff measured child height using a fixed stadiometer at the time of PFT assessment; age was also recorded at this time. We collected maternal residential addresses throughout pregnancy, beginning with address at enrollment, and characterized neighborhood-level resources using the Child Opportunity Index (COI).25 A time-weighted average COI score was calculated for each woman based on all reported addresses during pregnancy.

### Statistical Analysis

We used multivariable linear regression to estimate beta coefficients and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI) to assess the association between maternal GDM and continuous lung function z-scores. Primary models adjusted for maternal age, highest level of educational attainment, race, prenatal smoking (tobacco), asthma history, pre-pregnancy BMI, parity, prenatal COI and child sex at birth, child height and age at PFT. As stated previously, lung function z-scores were calculated by standardizing child sex, height and age to an external reference population,20 however we also included those factors as terms in our multivariable regression models to address any residual correlation within the CANDLE cohort.19 To supplement this approach, we conducted additional sensitivity analyses without adjustment for child sex, height and age. Acknowledging that race is a social and not a biologic construct, we adjusted for maternal race as it may serve as a proxy for health inequities resulting from systemic racism that may contribute to both GDM and lung function. We adjusted for pregnancy-related factors (gestational hypertension and gestational weight gain) and restricted to term births (gestational age ≥ 37 weeks) in separate sensitivity analyses. We did not adjust for birth weight, cesarean delivery, breastfeeding or other postnatal/childhood factors due to their potential to be on the causal pathway between GDM and respiratory outcomes.

We used multivariable logistic regression to estimate the association between maternal GDM and childhood current wheeze and asthma at age 8–9. Models were adjusted for maternal age, education, race, prenatal tobacco use, asthma history, pre-pregnancy BMI, parity, prenatal COI and child sex and age at assessment. Similar to our approach to the lung function analyses, we adjusted for gestational hypertension and gestational weight gain, and restricted to term births, in separate sensitivity analyses.

We used SAS version 9.4 (Cary, North Carolina) for data management and R version 4.4.1 (The R Foundation, Vienna, Austria) for analyses. A two-sided type 1 error rate of 0.05 delineated statistical significance.

## Results

### Gestational Diabetes and Childhood Pulmonary Function

Among the 722 dyads that completed the PFT assessment with acceptable effort (Table 1), 66% of women identified as Black/African American and 34% identified as non-Black (33% White, 0.5% Asian, and 0.5% Other); almost all identified as non-Hispanic (n = 705, 98%). Fifty-six percentof women had a high school education or less, and 60% were parous at enrollment. Women had a median age at enrollment of 26 years (interquartile range [IQR]: 22, 31). Fifty percent of children were male.

We identified 45 cases of GDM (6%). Women with GDM were older (median age at enrollment 31 vs. 26 years) and had higher pre-pregnancy BMI (30.5 vs. 25.9 kg/m2) than those without GDM. They were also more likely to deliver via cesarean (49% vs 34%) and their infants had slightly earlier gestational age at delivery (38.5 weeks vs. 39.2 weeks).

Median child age at PFT assessment was 8.8 years (IQR: 8.2, 9.3). In general, PFT scores skewed low relative to the global reference, with a median (IQR) FEV1 z-score of −0.47 (−1.14, 0.22), FVC z-score of −0.41 (−1.11, 0.31), FEV1/FVC z-score of −0.08 (−0.83, 0.61) and FEF25–75 z-score of −0.34 (−1.02, 0.38) (Table 2). In unadjusted comparisons (n = 722), we observed no difference in PFT z-scores among those with and without maternal GDM (FEV1 β = −0.01 (95% CI: −0.33, 0.30); FVC β = 0.16 (95% CI: −0.15, 0.47); FEV1/FVC β = −0.25 (95% CI: −0.59, 0.10); FEF25–75 β = −0.27 (95% CI: −0.59, 0.05), comparing children exposed to maternal GDM to those unexposed (referent)). We observed similar findings when the unadjusted analysis was restricted to those with complete data on all primary adjustment covariates (n = 713) (eTable 1). Following adjustment for primary covariates, the difference in FEV1 and FEF25–75 z-scores increased among children exposed to maternal GDM relative to those unexposed, corresponding to a decrease of −0.28 (95% CI: −0.56, −0.00) and −0.43 (95% CI: −0.76, −0.10), respectively. Results did not appreciably change for other outcomes following covariate adjustment (Table 3). Additional adjustment for gestational hypertension or gestational weight gain, or restriction to term births, yielded only modest fluctuations in estimates (eTable 1).

### Gestational Diabetes and Childhood Wheeze and Asthma

We identified 53 cases of GDM (6%) among the 892 dyads that completed the wheeze and asthma assessment. Overall demographic characteristics were similar to the CANDLE subset described for the PFT analysis (eTable 2). Descriptively, a higher proportion of children with maternal GDM exposure reported current wheeze and asthma as compared to those without maternal GDM exposure (current wheeze: 21% vs. 13%; current asthma: 26% vs 13%) (eTable 3), yielding unadjusted odds ratios of 1.85 (95% CI: 0.92, 3.70) and 2.47 (95% CI: 1.30, 4.70), respectively (Table 4). After adjustment for covariates, odds ratios increased to 2.23 (95% CI: 1.05, 4.73) and 3.12 (95% CI: 1.55, 6.28) for current wheeze and current asthma, respectively. Additional adjustment for gestational hypertension or gestational weight gain did not substantially change results (eTable 4). Odds ratios were slightly attenuated when analyses were restricted to term births (excluding 71 births) (2.02 (95% CI: 0.90, 4.56) for current wheeze and 2.90 (95% CI: 1.38, 6.10) for current asthma).

## Discussion

In this prospective cohort study of 8- to 9-year-old children and their mothers, we observed decrements in FEV1 and FEF25–75 among children born to mothers who had GDM. FEV1, is a reliable and clinically relevant measure of lung function that is used clinically as marker of airway obstruction. It is distinct from asthma and wheeze, as children with asthma may or may not have reduced FEV1 based on the degree of disease severity, control and other factors, and children without asthma may have decreased FEV1.26 GDM was associated with a modest decrease in baseline FEV1 in children and further research is needed to determine if this finding translates into early adulthood lung function deficits that have been associated with long-term respiratory decline. Similarly, FEF25–75 is a marker of airflow in the peripheral airways; it has debated clinical significance but has been associated with asthma and COPD in some studies.27 28 We also observed increased relative odds of asthma and wheeze among children born to mothers who had GDM, consistent with prior findings in this cohort at age 4–6 years of age.6 Taken collectively, the pattern of findings across these outcomes represent consistent evidence of an association between GDM and respiratory health in offspring.

Only one prior study to our knowledge has assessed GDM and childhood lung function.13 This prospective cohort of 889 mother-infant dyads in Wuhan, China reported associations between GDM and decreases in FEV1, FVC and FEF25–75 at approximately age 6. These findings are generally consistent with ours with the exception that our study did not observe substantially lower FVC. This study also determined that mid-pregnancy 1 and 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test levels were inversely associated with lung function measures, supporting the hypothesis that maternal hyperglycemia is associated with childhood lung function.

Studies of GDM or maternal diabetes and childhood asthma and wheeze are more common. Two recent meta-analyses determined overall effect estimates for the association between maternal diabetes and childhood asthma as 1.22 (95% CI: 1.07, 1.39) (gestational diabetes)7 and 1.13 (95% CI: 1.101, 1.27) (any maternal diabetes).8 Nasreen et al. described the association between GDM and childhood asthma in nearly 20,000 subjects in Canada’s National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth, reporting a hazard ratio of 1.25 (95% CI: 1.03, 1.51).16 Similarly, in a large Chinese study, Ma et al. reported an increased likelihood of childhood asthma when women experienced pregnancy complications, including gestational diabetes, hypertension and anemia; the odds ratio for GDM alone was 1.71 (95% CI: 1.65, 1.78).15 In contrast to these reports, a large population-based study in Israel determined no association between GDM and respiratory hospitalizations in offspring.29 Other studies have observed evidence of effect modification in the association of maternal diabetes and asthma/wheeze. Martinez et al.,14 observed that maternal type 2 diabetes and GDM requiring medication were both significantly associated with childhood asthma but GDM not requiring medication was not. Dumas et al.,30 reported an association between GDM and asthma by age 5 that was only observed among dyads with normal maternal pre-pregnancy BMI (odds ratio: 2.31, 95% CI: 1.46–3.65).

Gestational diabetes is associated with many complex processes that may disrupt healthy fetal development and the mechanism linking GDM to long-term perturbation in the lung is unclear. Broadly, elevated inflammation and oxidative stress are associated with diabetes and are also likely to influence fetal lung development.11 31 32 Another hypothesis proposes that excessive fetal insulin and insulin-like growth factors (IGF), produced as a result of fetal exposure to excessive maternal glucose (hyperglycemia), may influence lung maturation.33 The fetal lung expresses insulin receptors that are later suppressed, suggesting that insulin or IGF may play an important role in early lung development and that hyperinsulinemia during vulnerable stages may result in developmental disruptions.34 35 We can also consider indirect mechanisms operating, for example, through childhood metabolic conditions that are associated with GDM, such as glucose intolerance.36 Elevated insulin concentrations in early childhood have been shown to predict the development of asthma.37 Pre-pubertal children with high levels of insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance demonstrate evidence of bronchial hyperresponsiveness, irrespective of BMI.38 In adults, diabetes and asthma are common comorbidities. Adults with diabetes who are treated with metformin, an oral anti-glycemic medication, or glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists have reduced incident asthma and asthma exacerbations relative to non-users or insulin users,39–41 while use of insulin has been associated with increased risk of asthma.42

Our study has many strengths. We used prospectively collected data and included medical chart review to document GDM cases. We present findings on GDM and child lung function which has not been investigated widely in prior studies. Spirometry testing provides an objective measure of lung function that may capture poorly controlled, sub-clinical or undiagnosed lung disease. Lung function tends to be stable over time and therefore can be a useful marker of long-term health risks when measured in early life. We performed high-quality spirometry testing and applied the most up-to-date race-neutral reference equations to generate z-scores, avoiding racial bias that is present in prior z-score estimations.20 We also contributed to existing evidence on the association between GDM and asthma following children into middle childhood using a validated self-report instrument.22 43 An additional strength is that the CANDLE cohort reflects many of the underlying characteristics of Shelby County, TN, a southern urban region that includes a majority Black population,18 a demographic that is often understudied despite large racial disparities in asthma and related outcomes.44

We also note some limitations. Relative to larger studies of population-based or administrative cohorts that are well-suited to study diagnosed conditions such as asthma, we have a comparatively small sample size and few observed cases of GDM. Due to small sample size, we are not powered to investigate potentially important modifiers, such as differences in association by infant sex,12 13 diabetes severity14 or maternal pre-pregnancy BMI that have been observed in the asthma literature.30 We were not able to assess glycemic control, diet and physical activity, utilization of medications or other features of GDM diagnosis and treatment. We also acknowledge possible unmeasured confounding by factors such as indoor and outdoor air quality. However, by utilizing data from our prospective pregnancy cohort, we were able to obtain standardized clinical measures of lung function as well as observe and control for many important confounders that may not be observable in some administrative data, including prenatal smoking, maternal ever asthma history, parity and certain demographics.

In conclusion, we observed decrements in several measures of lung function in children with prenatal GDM exposure. Additionally, we observed associations between GDM and current asthma and wheeze in children at age 8–9 years, suggesting persistence of the diagnosis into middle childhood. GDM is already recognized as a risk factor for multiple pregnancy complications and childhood morbidities, such as obesity and type 2 diabetes10. This study highlights a possible relationship between GDM and childhood lung function, which is a meaningful indicator for long term health. However, as our study is based on few GDM exposed pregnancies, continued investigation into the long-term impacts of GDM on offspring respiratory development and health outcomes in larger studies is needed.

## Abstract

We investigated the individual and interaction effects of maternal plasma α- and γ-tocopherol levels (vitamin E isomers) on child asthma and wheeze at age 8–9.

Mother-child dyads were enrolled between 2006–2011 into the Conditions Affecting Neurocognitive Development and Learning in Early Childhood (CANDLE) prenatal cohort. Maternal 2nd trimester samples were analyzed for tocopherol and lipid concentrations. We assessed child asthma/wheeze using the International Study of Asthma and Allergies in Childhood (ISAAC) and other self-reported questionnaires and derived four outcome variables: (1) ever, (2) current, and (3) strict current asthma, (4) current wheeze. In multivariable logistic regression analyses we assessed associations of vitamin E isomers and child asthma/wheeze outcomes (n=847 mother-child dyads) and tested for pre-specified interaction terms.

Median cholesterol-corrected tocopherol levels [interquartile range (IQR)] were 5.0 (4.3–5.7) and 0.8 (0.7–0.9) (umol/mmol) for α- and γ-tocopherol, respectively. Associations between α-tocopherol and asthma outcome variables were inverse but not statistically significant. In contrast, for γ-tocopherol associations were in the positive direction, but also non-significant. Interactions analysis between tocopherols did not reach statistical significance for any outcome. Among children of women with a history of asthma, the likelihood of ever asthma in the child appears to be decreasing with increasing maternal α-tocopherol levels whereas this trend was not observed among those without a history of asthma (p-interaction=0.05).

We observed no associations for prenatal α- or γ-tocopherol concentrations with child asthma/wheeze. We detected some evidence of effect modification by maternal asthma history in associations between α-tocopherol and child asthma.

## Introduction

Asthma is a common chronic condition which affects an estimated 7 million US children.1 Recent research has focused on the hypothesis that inflammation and oxidative stress initiated in utero and during early life may play important roles in asthma development. Maternal prenatal dietary intake could impact childhood respiratory health through effects on inflammation and oxidative stress and by influencing early immune system development and predisposition to asthma-related disorders.2, 3

Vitamin E is a potent lipid soluble antioxidant which plays a role in mitigating oxidative stress and inflammation and in protecting cell membranes from free radical damage.4 Vitamin E exists as eight isomers, alpha- (α-), beta-, gamma- (γ-), and delta-tocopherols and tocotrienols. Although α-tocopherol is thought to have the highest biological activity and is usually included in supplements, γ-tocopherol is the predominant form in the US diet5 with higher levels found in nuts, seeds, whole grains, and vegetable oils.3 Supplement users generally have higher blood α- and lower γ-tocopherol concentrations; in part, because blood lipid concentrations influence levels of vitamin E and these two isomers compete for hepatic lipoprotein transport.6,7 This has led to recommendations that when vitamin E concentrations are used as an indicator of dietary intake, they should be adjusted for blood cholesterol.8

Animal models have demonstrated protective effects of vitamin E on allergic lung inflammation,7 with some studies suggesting differential, possibly antagonistic effects, for α- and γ-tocopherol. In mice, allergic inflammation decreased with α-tocopherol but increased with γ-tocopherol supplementation and the anti-inflammatory actions of α-tocopherol declined with higher γ-tocopherol levels,3 highlighting that these isomers should be considered concomitantly.

Two epidemiological studies of early life Vitamin E and child asthma have adopted this approach.9, 10 Project Viva9 measured tocopherols in 2nd trimester maternal and child plasma samples (n=622 mother-child dyads) and observed that higher α-tocopherol levels in childhood were positively associated with lung function but only when γ-tocopherol levels were low. Maternal concentrations of tocopherols (i.e. in utero child exposure) were not consistently associated with child spirometry parameters.9 The Infant Susceptibility to Pulmonary Infections and Asthma Following RSV Exposure (INSPIRE)11 examined the association between maternal postpartum α- and γ-tocopherol blood levels with child wheeze. Among 652 mother-child dyads higher postpartum maternal α-tocopherol concentrations were associated with a lower likelihood of wheezing in children. In contrast, γ-tocopherol concentrations were not associated with wheezing, and the protective association for α-tocopherol was attenuated among those with higher γ-tocopherol levels.10 While these results are intriguing, neither study corrected tocopherols for blood cholesterol concentrations or assessed whether the association between prenatal vitamin E status and child asthma was modified by biological factors such as child sex or maternal asthma/atopic disease, a marker of a familial predisposition to atopy.

This research investigated the individual and interactive effects of maternal 2nd trimester plasma α- and γ-tocopherol levels corrected for cholesterol status on child asthma and wheeze at 8–9 years in mother-child dyads enrolled in the CANDLE prenatal prospective cohort study. A priori, we planned to assess potential effect modification by maternal asthma history and child sex. This research will contribute to efforts aimed at the primary prevention of childhood asthma, while providing greater insight into the mechanisms surrounding atopic disease pathogenesis.

## Methods

### Study Population

CANDLE is a prospective pregnancy cohort that enrolled approximately 1500 mother-child pairs between 2006 to 2011 in Shelby County, Tennessee (Memphis area).12 Pregnant women were recruited during the 2nd trimester from community obstetric practices and an obstetric clinic and reflected the demographics of the County, which is roughly 2/3 African American and 1/3 White with a high proportion of low-income families.13 To be eligible, women had to be County residents between 16–40 years of age, at 16–27 weeks of gestation with a singleton and low medical risk pregnancyand able to speak and understand English.12, 14 For this investigation, dyads with infant estimated gestational age (EGA) <32 weeks were excluded to limit potential confounding from prematurity-associated lung disease. CANDLE child participants have been followed prospectively through ages 8–9 years. Study procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center (UTHSC), Vanderbilt University and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. Women 18 years of age and older provided informed consent while those under 18 years of age provided assent with consent provided by their legally authorized representative. Children participating in this investigation provided assent.

### Child Asthma and Wheeze Assessment

We defined asthma/wheeze outcomes using the International Study of Asthma and Allergies in Childhood (ISAAC)15 and other self-reported questionnaires administered at 8–9 years. Ever asthma was defined as an affirmative response to “Has a physician or other health care provider ever told your family that your child had asthma or reactive airway disease?” Current asthma was defined as an affirmative response to 2 out of 3 of the following questions: “Has a physician or other health care provider ever told your family that your child had asthma or reactive airway disease?” “Has your child ever had wheezing or whistling in the chest in the last 12 months?” and/or ”In the past 12 months, has your child used any type of medicines, liquids, puffers or other medication for wheezing or asthma?” Strict current asthma was defined as an affirmative response to “Has a physician or other health care provider ever told your family that your child had asthma or reactive airway disease?” and either a) report of current wheezing, or b) asthma medication use in the past 12 months. Current wheeze was defined as affirmative response to “Had wheezing or whistling in the chest in the last 12 months.”14, 16

### Vitamin E Assessment

Our primary predictor variables were prenatal plasma tocopherol concentrations corrected for blood lipid (i.e., cholesterol) concentrations, expressed as umol tocopherol / mmol cholesterol, or umol/mmol.17 Plasma α- and γ-tocopherol levels were measured in 2nd trimester maternal blood specimens. Tocopherols were assayed via HPLC and total cholesterol via an enzymatic method in the Molecular Epidemiology and Biomarker Research at the University of Minnesota (Dr. Myron Gross, Director; Hannah Carlson, Project Manager).18, 19 We ran two control samples for each type of analysis. Inter-assay CVs for γ-tocopherol were 4.7% at 0.151 mg/dL, and 7.0% at 0.171 mg/dL and 8.5% at 0.797 mg/dL, and 8.8% at .741 mg/dL for α-tocopherol. Total cholesterol was measured on a Roche COBAS 8000 chemistry analyzer. For cholesterol, the inter-assay CVs were 4% at 168 mg/dL and 1.1% at 258 mg/dL. We defined adequacy of plasma α-tocopherol as ≥ 30 umol/L; McBurney and colleagues6 derived a cutoff for adequacy for cholesterol-corrected α-tocopherol of 5.8 (umol/mmol) from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data. Criteria for adequacy for γ-tocopherol have not been established.

### Covariates

At enrollment, information on maternal age, race (self-reported Black/African American, White, other), educational attainment (<high school, high school/GED, colloge degree / technical school, >college degree), self-reported asthma history (yes/no), parity (primiparous/multiparous), smoking during pregnancy (yes/no) and pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI (weight (kg)/ height (m2)) were collected. Data collected at birth included gestational weight gain (kg), delivery type (vaginal, cesarean), sex (male, female), and estimated gestational age (weeks). Duration of any (none, <6 months, ≥6 months) and exclusive breastfeeding (none, < 6 months, ≥6 months) and presence of pets in the home were assessed by questionnaire at 4–6 years of age.

### Statistical Analysis

A total of 912 dyads had primary outcome variables available. Of these, 18 were excluded due to birth < 32 weeks. Exposure (levels of tocopherols and cholesterol) data were available for 847 women yielding a final analytic dataset of 847 dyads. Univariate and bivariate descriptive analysis of exposure, outcome and covariate data were conducted and we evaluated the distributions of potential confounders across quintiles of plasma α- and γ-tocopherol. Our primary models were adjusted for a priori selected covariates14,16, similar to what we have reported previously: maternal age, race, educational status, parity and pre-pregnancy BMI and child sex and age (years) at the 8–9 year visit.

In separate multivariable logistic regression models, we investigated the association of α- and γ-tocopherol as log transformed continuous and categorical predictors (quintiles) with asthma/wheeze outcomes. We also evaluated non-linear associations using restricted cubic splines. Wald tests (P=overall) were used to test overall effects of tocopherols in the models. We tested for pre-specified interaction between α- and Y-tocopherol by including cross-product terms first using quintiles and then using continuous measures expanded with non-linear terms using restricted cubic splines. In separate multivariable regression models, we tested for potential effect modification by (1) maternal atopy (ever; yes/no), and (2) child sex, on the relationship between α- or Y-tocopherol exposure variables and child wheeze/asthma outcomes by including the relevant interaction term.

In sensitivity analyses, we included weight gain during pregnancy and duration of exclusive breastfeeding as covariates in our fully-adjusted models. Additionally, we modeled associations between α- and γ-tocopherol with asthma outcomes without correction for cholesterol to allow for direct comparisons to previously reported results by others and analyzed the associations of interest using the α- and γ-tocopherol ratio as a measure of exposure. Analyses were performed in R Version 4.2.1 (Vienna, Austria) with statistical significance at the 2-sided level alpha level of 0.05.

## Results

In our sample of 847 mother-child dyads, parents reported ever asthma in 18.3%, current asthma in 13.5%, strict asthma in 11.3% and current wheeze in 12.9% of children. Approximately 65% of women were African American and 12% reported a history of asthma. About 37% and 28% of mothers met criteria for adequacy of plasma α-tocopherol and cholesterol-corrected α-tocopherol concentrations, respectively. The Spearman non-parametric correlation coefficient between α- and γ-tocopherol concentrations was ρ=0.15 for raw levels and ρ=0.11 (both P<0.001) for cholesterol-corrected tocopherol levels. Compared with women who had higher concentrations of α-tocopherol, those with lower levels tended to be younger and more likely to be African American; however, for γ-tocopherol, women with lower levels tended to be older and less likely to be African American (Table 1).

The associations between quintiles of α-tocopherol and our four asthma outcome variables (Table 2) were in the protective direction (inverse) but none reached statistical significance and 95% CIs were wide. In contrast, for quintiles of γ-tocopherol, the associations were trending in the positive direction and non-significant. Sensitivity analyses which additionally adjusted models for gestational weight gain and duration of exclusive breast feeding generated similar results. In sensitivity analyses conducted with expanded nonlinear terms, with low levels of γ-tocopherol (but not high), we observed the suggestion of a curvilinear protective effect for α-tocopherol with strict asthma (Supplemental Figure 1); however, the 95% CI bands for risk estimates overlapped. In covariate adjusted models, interactions for α- and γ-tocopherol did not reach statistical significance for any asthma outcome variables. Additional analyes using the ratio of α-tocopherol:γ-tocopherol as the measure of exposure yielded consistent results (Supplemental Table 1).

There were no significant interactions observed by sex with either tocopherol for any asthma/wheeze outcomes. For maternal atopy, we observed a significant interaction for the ever asthma outcome with α-tocopherol in the adjusted model (p interaction=0.05). For children of women with an asthma history, the likelihood of ever asthma appeared to decrease with increasing α-tocopherol; this trend was not observed among women without an asthma history (Figure 1A). We did not observe significant interactions between maternal atopy history and α-tocopherol for the other three outcomes.

Lastly, we conducted sensitivity analyses to assess associations between α- and γ-tocopherol with asthma/wheeze outcome variables utilizing tocopherol variables with raw value measures (without cholesterol correction) to allow for comparisons with results of previous investigations. Overall, these demonstrated a similar pattern (not presented) to our reported results.

## Discussion

In this large diverse prospective prenatal cohort study, we did not find evidence for robust associations for either maternal 2nd trimester α- or γ-tocopherol concentrations with child asthma/wheeze at eight years of age. Among women with a history of asthma, the likelihood of child ever asthma, but not other outcomes, was lower with higher α-tocopherol concentrations, but there was no association among women without asthma. This finding, in particular, requires examination in other populations as it suggests that α-tocopherol could have a role in buffering risk of intergenerational transmission of risk.

Previous research examining pregnancy vitamin E measures in relation to child respiratory outcomes has produced mixed results. Prior studies did not correct tocopherol levels for cholesterol concentrations and one study collected blood specimens at a postpartum visit via finger stick. In a Massachusetts cohort, Kumar et al.9 evaluated associations between maternal 2nd trimester plasma tocopherols in relation to spirometry measures in children at ages 6–10 years (n=622). Maternal tocopherol levels were not consistently associated with child spirometry parameters in multivariable models.9 In another prospective birth cohort in Tennessee, Stone et al.11 analyzed the association between maternal postpartum finger stick blood samples analyzed for α- and γ-tocopherol with child wheeze or asthma medication receipt in the past 12 months or parent reported child asthma diagnosis (n=652). Higher α-tocopherol concentrations were associated with a lower likelihood of wheezing (OR for interquartile range increase = 0.70 (95% CI: 0.53, 0.92)); γ-tocopherol concentrations were not associated with wheezing (OR=0.79; 95% CI: 0.56, 1.10). Further, the protective association for α-tocopherol was attenuated among those with higher γ-tocopherol levels (p-interaction=0.05).10

Vitamin E levels in this population were similar to those observed in previous research and in US nationally representative data. Recommended intakes for vitamin E for pregnant women are 15 mg/day (as α-tocopherol) and are set to result in serum α-tocopherol levels of approximately 27.9 umol/L (1.2017 mg/dL).20 Although national surveys have reported that most adults do not meet the recommendations for vitamin E intakes, deficiency (defined as serum < 12 umol/L or 0.5169 mg/dL) symptoms are rare.6 No women in the current study had vitamin E levels < 12 umol/L.

Possible interpretations for our interaction results suggesting that the potential protective effect of higher α-tocopherol concentrations related to childhood asthma development is limited to women with asthma history could be that the potential for protective effects is more likely to be observed among those at higher risk. Previous research has shown that childhood asthma may be more common among children of women with uncontrolled asthma during pregnancy.18, 21, 22 Another possibility is that maternal atopy or the medications to treat this condition may affect the bioavailability or metabolism of α-tocopherol thereby contributing to protective effects. In this study, women in the lowest quintile of α-tocopherol were the least likely to report a history of asthma (8% in the lowest v. 13% in the highest quintile). Lastly, we cannot rule out the possibility that the observed differences could be due to chance; however, in previous analyses in the CANDLE cohort we observed related results. Maternal n-6 PUFA concentrations were positively associated with child respiratory outcomes in main effects models, and in interaction models, increasing n-6 PUFAS were associated with higher risk of respiratory outcomes only among children of women with asthma history.14

This study has a number of strengths and some potential limitations. Our analyses were conducted in a well-characterized, large, ethnically diverse prospective cohort and utilized objectively measured exposures. Samples measured for tocopherols were all collected at a similar time during pregnancy and adjusted for blood lipid concentrations. Limitations of this study include that tocopherol measures were analyzed at only one time during pregnancy. We used parent-reported questionnaire data to derive our child asthma/wheeze variables; however, these questions have been previously validated.23 Nevertheless, although we include one measure of a familial predisposition to develop asthma, maternal asthma, there are likely some children in the group of dyads without maternal asthma who have a first degree relative with asthma. While we controlled for a number of potential confounders and assessed several possible effect modifiers, the possibility of unmeasured confounding or effect modifying variables that may have influenced our results cannot be ruled out.

This study adds to the research assessing prenatal diet as an important consideration in the development of child respiratory diseases. Future research should include investigations of these biomarkers across multiple time points in pregnancy and address the role of prenatal vitamin E status in child respiratory disease development at other ages and using objective outcomes and/or physician diagnosed asthma/wheeze.
